title: Growing swede
subtitle: A hardy brassica root sown in May or June for winter storage
excerpt: Swede is sown direct in May or June and left to swell through the summer and autumn. It tolerates hard frosts and can be left in the ground through winter, lifted as needed. Brassica rotation and butterfly netting at the seedling stage are the key requirements.
sourceNotes: RHS swede growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), root vegetable section. USDA cooperative extension notes on rutabaga production, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: The part of the swede above the widest point of the root, below the crown of leaves. A thick, well-developed neck indicates a healthy bulky root. Swedes with a long thin neck and poor root development have usually grown too fast on over-rich soil. The neck can become stringy if the root is left in the ground well past maturity.

content.text: Swede needs a long growing season; sow in May or June for harvest from October. It is one of the hardiest root vegetables and can be left in the ground through winter in most of the UK, lifted as required. Like all brassicas, it needs a strict rotation and protection from cabbage white butterflies at the seedling stage.

Sow direct in the growing position from late May to late June. Sowing outdoors in rows at 1 cm deep; thin in two stages to a final spacing of 23 to 25 cm between plants, with rows 38 to 45 cm apart. Transplanting swede causes root distortion and is not recommended. Cover the seedlings with fine netting for the first six weeks to protect from flea beetle and cabbage white butterfly.

Full sun, firm, fertile soil. Swede does not need a freshly manured bed; rich conditions cause lush leafy growth at the expense of root development. A reasonable, weed-free bed with a general fertiliser applied before sowing is sufficient. pH 6.0 to 7.0. Apply lime if the soil is acid; clubroot is more severe in acid conditions.

Swede largely looks after itself once established. Water in prolonged dry spells during July and August when roots are developing; erratic watering causes the roots to split. Keep the bed weed-free; large weeds can distort root development. The
should be well developed and the root firm before harvest.

Swede is ready from October when the roots are 10 to 15 cm in diameter. It can be left in the ground through winter and lifted as needed; frost improves the flavour. In very cold areas or on heavy wet soils, lift and store in a frost-free shed in sand or straw by Christmas. Roots left in the ground too long become woody.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The main swede problems in UK growing.

items.symptom: Seedlings eaten or peppered with small holes
items.cause: Flea beetle, most active in dry weather.
items.fix: Cover seedlings with fine insect-proof mesh. Flea beetle damage is worst in dry conditions; water the seedlings to keep them growing vigorously through the vulnerable stage.

items.cause: Erratic watering or heavy rain after a dry period.
items.fix: Water consistently during the root-swelling period in July and August. Mulch to retain moisture.
